summary:
Treck to Jezero is an interactive Mars exploration and route-planning web system that helps future human explorers understand and evaluate the Martian surface. Focused on Jezero Crater, it combines observations and datasets from multiple NASA missions, including data collected by the Perseverance rover, into a unified 3D and 2D visualization.
Users can explore the terrain interactively, examine a proposed 4-kilometer traverse across five scientific waypoints, and investigate geological features under different environmental and surface conditions. Scientific layers include elevation, slope, thermal inertia, radiation, temperature, and potential terrain hazards.
The system introduces two complementary assessments. The Ancient Habitability Score (AHS) explores evidence of past environments that may have supported microbial life. The Human Habitability Score (HHS) evaluates environmental and terrain-related factors relevant to future human exploration.
By turning complex planetary science data into an accessible, interactive experience, Treck to Jezero supports scientific understanding, mission planning research, and public education. It also deonstrates how integrated planetary data can help humans prepare for future Mars exploration.
Treck to Jezero is an educational research prototype. Its assessments and proposed routes are exploratory visualizations, not certified astronaut navigation or safety recommendations.
details:
What it does?

Treck to Jezero is an interactive planetary exploration application that brings together scientific information about Jezero Crater, Mars, into a single environment. It allows users to explore the Martian surface in 3D, follow a proposed traverse, examine geological features, and investigate the conditions that may influence scientific exploration and future human activities.

Rather than presenting terrain as a simple map, Treck to Jezero organizes available NASA observations into different scientific layers. Users can examine elevation, slope, mineralogy, thermal properties, environmental observations, potential terrain hazards, and data coverage to better understand the area. The application is designed for educational exploration and scientific visualization. It does not provide certified astronaut navigation or guarantee that a proposed location is safe for human activity.

How it Works?

1. Interactive terrain and route visualization.

The main interface features an interactive 3D representation of Jezero Crater, accompanied by a floating 2D route overview. Users can rotate, pan, zoom, and inspect the terrain while following the proposed exploration route. The planned traverse covers approximately 4.0 km and contains five waypoints:

  • Three Forks / Hogwallow Flats (0.0 km): Examines sedimentary environments, layered mudstones, and evidence associated with ancient water activity.
  • South Séítah Margin (approximately 1.4 km): Focuses on water-altered minerals, rocky outcrops, and nearby loose terrain.
  • Artuby Ridge (approximately 2.3 km): Highlights geological boundaries, mineral diversity, and terrain accessibility.
  • Máaz Formation Flats (approximately 3.2 km): Examines basaltic plains, surface properties, and environmental considerations.
  • Octavia E. Butler Landing (approximately 4.0 km): Presents a proposed location for evaluating terrain flatness, boulder distribution, and potential landing or habitat considerations.

The 2D and 3D views are designed to work together, allowing users to select waypoints and examine the corresponding locations and information.

2. Scientific map layers

Treck to Jezero organizes available scientific observations into independently selectable layers:

  • Elevation and Topography: Shows variations in the Martian surface using available elevation products.
  • Slope and Accessibility: Highlights terrain gradients that may influence movement across the surface.
  • Ancient Habitability: Presents geological and mineralogical evidence associated with past water activity and potential preservation of biosignatures.
  • Human Habitability: Organizes environmental and terrain factors relevant to possible future human exploration.
  • Thermal Inertia: Provides information about surface thermal properties.
  • Mineralogy: Highlights supported observations of minerals such as clay, carbonates, olivine, and sulfates.
  • Radiation: Presents relevant radiation information while distinguishing measurements collected at other locations from direct Jezero observations.
  • Temperature and Wind: Displays available environmental observations from the Perseverance mission.
  • Dust and Soil Hazards: Organizes available information about dust, loose terrain, and supported soil-related observations.
  • Hazard Exclusion Zones: Highlights potential concerns such as steep slopes, loose sand, dunes, and dense boulder fields where supported by available information.
  • Confidence and Data Coverage: Shows where observations are available, incomplete, uncertain, or missing.

Each scientific layer is intended to provide its own legend, explanation, data source, and availability information.

3. Ancient and Human Habitability Assessment

Treck to Jezero introduces two team-developed exploratory assessments:

  • Ancient Habitability Score (AHS): Organizes evidence related to past liquid water, water-formed minerals, geological chemistry, preservation potential, and available organic detections.
  • Human Habitability Score (HHS): Organizes factors relevant to future human exploration, including radiation information, temperature, wind, terrain accessibility, surface properties, dust, and soil-related hazards.

Users can explore different mission profiles that change the relative emphasis placed on AHS and HHS. These scores are project-derived educational models, not official NASA measurements or validated predictions of habitability. Their interpretation depends on the availability, quality, and limitations of the underlying observations.

4. Data confidence and transparency

An important part of Treck to Jezero is communicating how much information is available for a particular area. The application distinguishes between available data, partial coverage, proxy information, derived results, simulated content, and unavailable datasets. This helps users understand the difference between direct observations and interpretations based on incomplete information. Missing observations are not automatically classified as safe or hazardous. Confidence categories are intended as display indicators and should not be interpreted as scientifically validated probabilities.

5. Educational exploration

Treck to Jezero is designed to make planetary science more accessible to the public. Users can explore individual waypoints, learn about geological features, understand the purpose of scientific instruments, and discover how different observations contribute to the study of Mars. The application connects scientific information with the proposed route so users can understand not only where an explorer might travel, but also what scientific questions could be investigated along the way.

Data and Scientific Approach

The project is based on NASA mission datasets and NASA-derived scientific products. These include orbital observations from Mars Global Surveyor, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, and Mars Odyssey, alongside relevant surface observations from the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers.

Different datasets provide different types of information. For example, elevation products support terrain visualization, mineralogical observations help identify geological features, and rover environmental measurements provide context about conditions on the Martian surface.

Some observations are not collected directly at Jezero Crater. Curiosity RAD measurements, for example, are treated as proxy information rather than direct radiation measurements from the proposed route. Historical environmental observations are also distinguished from current or live conditions.

Development Tools and Technologies

Treck to Jezero was developed using the following tools and technologies:

  • HTML: Used to structure the application's interface and organize its different sections, interactive elements, and information displays.
  • Python: Used for data-related operations, including working with scientific datasets and supporting the organization and processing of information used in the application.
  • Codex: Used as an AI-assisted development tool to support the coding process, help implement application features, and assist with development and debugging.

These technologies helped the team develop an interactive platform that brings together scientific information, terrain visualization, and educational features in one application.

Creativity and Innovation

The creativity of Treck to Jezero comes from how it combines different types of planetary science information into a single interactive exploration experience. Instead of presenting NASA datasets as separate maps, charts, or technical documents, the application organizes them into connected scientific layers that users can explore through a 3D representation of Jezero Crater.

Another creative aspect is the integration of the Ancient Habitability Score and Human Habitability Score. These team-developed assessments provide an educational way to examine Jezero Crater from two different perspectives: its potential to have supported ancient microbial life and its relevance to possible future human exploration.

The application also emphasizes data transparency by showing the availability, limitations, and confidence of different observations. This allows users to understand not only what the available scientific information suggests, but also where information is incomplete or uncertain.

Factors Considered During Development

The team considered several factors to ensure that Treck to Jezero would be informative, understandable, and responsible in presenting scientific information:

  • Scientific Accuracy: Prioritized NASA mission datasets and distinguished actual observations from team-derived assessments, proxy measurements, and simulated information.
  • Data Availability: Considered the coverage, quality, and limitations of available scientific observations, especially when certain measurements were not collected directly at Jezero Crater.
  • User Experience: Designed the interface to make complex planetary science information easier to explore through interactive maps, selectable layers, and organized explanations.
  • Terrain and Environmental Conditions: Considered elevation, slope, geological features, temperature, wind, radiation information, dust, and other factors relevant to planetary exploration.
  • Educational Value: Ensured that the application could help students and the public understand Mars, scientific observations, and the challenges of planning future exploration.
  • Responsible Interpretation: Avoided presenting exploratory scores, incomplete observations, or proposed routes as officially validated NASA assessments or guaranteed safety recommendations.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Future human explorers will need to understand the terrain, geological characteristics, and environmental conditions of their destinations before and during surface exploration. Treck to Jezero demonstrates how information from different NASA missions can be brought together into one interactive environment.

By combining terrain visualization, scientific layers, habitability assessments, and data transparency, the project helps users understand the complexity of evaluating a potential Mars exploration route. It also provides an educational way for students and the public to explore Jezero Crater and learn how planetary scientists use mission data to investigate the history and potential habitability of Mars.

Important Limitations

Treck to Jezero is an educational visualization and research prototype. Its proposed route and habitability assessments are not certified astronaut navigation or safety recommendations. The application distinguishes actual NASA-derived observations from team-calculated scores, proxy measurements, illustrative content, and unavailable information. Simulated terrain or illustrative values, where used, must be clearly identified and must not be presented as measured scientific data.
